As hon. members will appreciate, there is a certain amount of overlap in the area of human resource management, in particular between the D'Avignon report and the Lambert commission report. That is the mechanism that I see at the present time.

Do I take it that the minister is telling us that apart from the D'Avignon and Lambert commission reports and the Public Service Staff Relations Act review-which is very important and which I think hon. members recognize was the object of serious study by this House and the Senate some three years ago-there are seven technical amendments concerning very important things to be done with reference to the Public Service Staff Relations Act? Am I to take it that the President of the Treasury Board is responsible for those amendments? In years past the President of the Privy Council was responsible. Do we take it that this has been changed and that Treasury Board is now responsible for reviewing its own Public Service Staff Relations Act?
Mr. Chairman, as I believe I indicated, the chairman of the cabinet committee with which ultimate responsibility rests in this regard is the President of the Privy Council.

One last question, Mr. Chairman, which deals with the question the minister alluded to a few minutes ago, and that is the retraining facilities offered to public servants who, due to either lack of work or for other reasons, are laid off. I know the minister is aware that the manpower retraining programs which apply to the general public do not apply to public servants who are laid off. I understand the reasons for that. As an employer, government was told to do its own retraining. Sometimes, however, there is a situation where a public servant is laid off because of lack of work or for other reasons and is not eligible for the retraining programs offered by Manpower.
Could the President of the Treasury Board give an assurance that this whole problem will be cleared up soon and that public servants will be offered retraining facilities and allowed to use Manpower programs?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. Under the rules he may ask questions later.

Mr. Chairperson, I agree with many of the things that the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier has said. We sit on the same miscellaneous estimates committee and some of the concerns he has expressed about the Public Service Commission are also my concern.
I should like to ask the President of the Treasury Board whether, in order to stop the overruns for training and development within the Public Service Commission, he would consider making departments responsible for paying for training which they indicate they require or sometimes request, so that the onus and accountability for spending for training and development are on the department and not on the Public Service Commission?

Mr. Chairman, as I recall, that Very matter is under review at the present time. I understand the validity of the point and I believe it should be followed up in order to put cost and responsibility together.

At the present time the amount that is being reviewed by the miscellaneous estimates committee on overruns is almost three-quarters of a million dollars and is projected to be over $1 million for the next two years and each year following. I think it is necessary that there be some change in the accountability for training that is offered and that it is placed on the departments. I hope the minister will see fit to do that.
1 should like now to turn to the Auditor General's report, the main thrust of which I felt was in the area of government spending and ineffective management. The media, however, seemed to place the blame on the inefficiency of public employees. I should like to know the minister's impression of the Auditor General's report and what it was trying to say to Parliament.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. gentleman knows, 1 have attempted, and I think successfully, not only to think through the comments of the Auditor General but to discuss them with my colleagues on both sides of the House.
In my judgment, and 1 believe in the judgment of the Auditor General, the problems of inefficiency in the groups examined, which were classes 1 to 4 of the clerical and regulatory groups, are management problems. In some of my answers to questions in this House I have emphasized that it is important that we not try to make the clerical and regulatory group the scapegoat of inefficiency. As anyone knows, if that group is not performing, not doing work assigned to them, or if they are inefficient, then we believe that is the responsibility of management.
The question the hon. member raises must be placed in the same context as the question raised by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, namely that we have a management problem, a human resource management problem. That is what we are attacking through the reforms which we hope to put in place and through the implementation of the D'Avignon and Lambert reports.
Would the minister agree that it is being said of the Auditor General's report that ineffective management is the problem and not, in fact, the inefficiency of public employees?

As a generalization that is my impression, Mr. Chairman. The management problem is the one to which we must address ourselves. I would not suggest for a moment that one does not find inefficiency here and there among employees, as one does everywhere, probably even in this House of Commons. We are going to address ourselves to this problem in terms of management, and I am satisfied that the Auditor General will support us in that because I believe that is what he would like to see.
May 14, 1980

1 thank the minister for his answer. 1 was sure that was his stand on the report as well as the stand of the Auditor General, but 1 just wanted that to go on the record to show that it is not inefficient public servants or inefficient public employees that sometimes make the systems go astray.
It has been mentioned that the problem of human resources and personnel management will be addressed and given a lot of consideration. I should like to know whether it is the intention of the Treasury Board to become responsible for personnel management and human resources as well as money management?

Mr. Chairman, in answer to that question, we are responsible for human resource management. We are responsible for the management of the human and financial resources of the government. What we are not responsible for at the present time is the staffing function, which rests with the Public Service Commission.
Mr. Chairman, to rephrase my question then, is it the intention of the Treasury Board to become involved in the staffing function of this government as well as the management of our money?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. gentleman probably knows, this question of where the staffing function rests has been addressed by the Lambert commission, by D'Avignon and by the Auditor General himself. Those three recommendations are that the staffing should rest with Treasury Board in terms of the over-all accountability of government for personnel and human resource management.
I would simply say at this stage that this is one of the recommendations which we are studying and which is under review, but we have not at this point in time made any firm commitment one way or the other with respect thereto.

Mr. Chairman, it was indicated in the public accounts for the year 1978-1979 that come out prior to the Auditor General's report that the spending deficit of the federal government for that year was $16,185 billion. That is the difference between the amount the government actually took in in revenue and the amount it actually spent out of the taxpayers' pocket.
I should like to know if the minister in fact finds this acceptable, and assuming that he will not find it acceptable, what the government plans to do to curb this deficit. Does it plan on increasing revenue or decreasing spending to lower that $16,185 billion deficit from 1979?

First of all, Mr. Chairman, 1 cannot verify the number which the hon. member has put forward. He is talking about last year. The hon. member for York-Peel a few moments ago was talking about what he thought was the projected deficit, but I hasten to add that there has been no fiscal planning projection put before this House. I think that point was made clear during the comments of the Minister of Finance.
Supply
With respect to the role of Treasury Board as it addresses itself to a problem such as the deficit, our mandate and our responsibility is to ensure that public funds are expended in a most effective and efficient manner. So the extent to which we can reduce expenditures will have an obvious impact on the deficit. As I pointed out many times, one can reduce a deficit either by reduced expenditures on the one hand or increased revenues on the other. That is a statement which requires no proof, if you like.
That being said, 1 can assure the hon. member that at Treasury Board we are consistently following policies of restraint, trying to identify inefficiencies and improve management practices. The Comptroller General, as you know, has his IMPAC study under way-that is, the Improvement of Management Practices and Controls-whereby effectively a survey is made of all major departments of government. That being done, then a report is made and eventually an action plan is agreed upon between the office of the Comptroller General and the deputy of that department. That action plan would then be implemented and monitored and address itself to all these various areas of management improvement practice with a view to obtaining greater efficiency, and with a view also to permitting us to establish techniques of evaluating programs in those departments so that informed judgments can be made by deputies and ministers with respect to the validity, the value of particular programs, and as to whether or not they are achieving their intended objectives.
So in this whole area of improved management, Treasury Board has a very active role to play, and to the extent that we can get at reducing the deficit through that role, we will certainly do so.

I thank the minister for the answer; I am not sure what he said there. The $16,185 billion is an actual figure and it comes from the public accounts for 1978-1979. I am surprised that the three gentlemen the minister has brought in here cannot substantiate that figure.
I should like to ask the minister this. If it is in keeping with government policy to reduce that deficit-and he did not say whether it would be increasing revenue or decreasing spending-are the cuts in the public service of some 5,840 person-years of employment that he announced when tabling the estimates in fact part of that policy?

I apologize, Mr. Chairman. I did not pay as much attention to the latter part of that question as I should have. With my apologies, 1 would appreciate it if the hon. member would just repeat the last part of that question, please.

With respect to the policy just stated in response to my question about the $16,185 billion deficit, I asked if the 5,840 or so person-years of employment were part of that new policy that he is planning on implementing to reduce the huge deficit.

Mr. Chairman, I indicated in this House earlier this week that it is not our policy to establish targets for

May 14, 1980
Supply
employee reduction. We do not intend to follow a policy, as my predecessor did, by saying, for example, that we are going to eliminate 60,000 public servants over a three-year period, partly as he suggested at the time by privatization of Crown corporations and then some in the control sector and some in the non-control sector of the public service. We have no such intention. What I am content to do is to attack inefficiencies and to evaluate and evolve programs.
In the course of that, it may be that by eliminating a program we will in fact lose some employees. At the same time, as I pointed out, we are very concerned about the position of employees who find themselves in surplus and subject to lay-off. It is for that reason, among many other reasons, that we are putting, I hope, a renewed and increased emphasis on retraining so as to find other positions for those employees in the public service.
That is the basic philosophy. It is not a question of saying that we are going to eliminate 5,000 or 10,000 jobs; it is a question of saying that we are going to attack inefficiencies. Surely the hon. gentleman will appreciate that a program which is being evaluated turns out basically not to be delivering a service to the public or to whomever it is intended to deliver to in the private or the public sector, it then behoves us to eliminate that program or to replace it with a more effective one. It is not unlikely that, in the course of doing that, the person-years would be affected. That is why we have this complementary program that I mentioned earlier of improved-and substantially improved, I hope-training and retraining.
Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the minister would answer this question. How was the criteria set, or what criteria was used to eliminate the 5,840 person-years of employment?
Mr. Chairman, again I apologize. Could I have that last sentence again? I am attempting to uncover where this $16.7 billion deficit which the gentleman referred to in 1978-79 occurred.
$16.1 billion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The President of the Treasury Board has the floor.
Mr. Chairperson, what criteria were used to eliminate the 5,840 person-years of employment that were cut from public employees?

Mr. Chairman, the person-year reduction the hon. member is referring to is that reduction which is contained and referred to in the main estimates which were tabled. I presume that is what he is referring to, namely 5,840 person-years, which reflects the policy of the previous Conservative administration.

Mr. Chairperson, I would like to have the President of the Treasury Board tell me if in fact some of those cuts were in the Canadian Transport Commission in areas of safety regulation, in fact areas where we had two unfortunate accidents lately, one at MacGregor, Manitoba, and the other at Mississauga, Ontario, in which lives were endangered and which involved great cost to the Canadian taxpayer in the clean-up. Have some of those cuts been made in that area? Whether or not it is the policy of the former Conservative government, does the minister not think this should be rethought and that possibly there should not be cuts in the Canadian Transport Commission, since Mr. Macdonell, in his Auditor General's report, said that is one of the areas that should be beefed up and not cut? The minister has in fact chosen to ignore that, I would guess, and will continue to make cuts in areas of safety regulations within the Canadian Transport Commission.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the Canadian Transport Commission cuts, those cuts, in the view of the commission, were made to achieve operational efficiency. I think it is presumptuous to assume that because of these cuts the safety of the Canadian public has in any way been endangered, or to attribute any accidents to the fact that these cuts took place. The hon. member is making an assumption which is certainly not warranted on the evidence before us at the moment.

I assure you, Mr. Chairperson, that the evidence is there. I would like to ask if the estimates that were tabled reflect any money to be paid out by way of incentives to senior bureaucrats to be attracted to this government.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to have some clarification as to what the hon. member means by "incentives to attract senior bureaucrats to the government." I am afraid I would need somewhat more information in order to respond to that in a meaningful way. What kind of incentives is the hon. member suggesting? Is he suggesting that we offer hiring bonuses to management groups? I am just not clear on the object of the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake has less than a minute to comment on that.

To my understanding, Treasury Board or officials under the President of the Treasury Board have discussed the possibility of making available large loans at extremely low interest rates in order to attract people to very senior public service positions. Is this in fact true and is it reflected in the estimates?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member's time has expired. He may have an opportunity later to pose his question.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak about my impressions as a new member of this House. I want to put before this committee what I perceive to be the position of the people I represent on certain vital issues and what they expect of me, of this government and of the Thirty-second Parlia-

Good policy.
May 14, 1980

ment. I want to do so in the context of the debate on public accounts. I hope hon. members will accept what I have to say as relevant to the issue under debate and the constructive manner in which these remarks are tendered. Some of the things which I feel I have to say may not be well received on either side of this House. This is most unfortunate because in my caucus-and I hope in saying what I do I am not breaching caucus secrecy-I am known as "Mr. Nice guy."
One thing I must say will be well received; it is easy for me to say and I mean it most sincerely. Speaking of members of all parties, I have been most impressed by the calibre, dedication and compassion of all members of this House. 1 say that without equivocation.
That having been said, may I now move on to my personal concerns and those of my riding, concerns which are strictly relevant to this debate this afternoon, concerns which, if justified, should be addressed by our Thirty-second Parliament and hopefully remedied. The perception of government today in my riding is that it is incapable of efficient legislative action; that it is so busy fighting fires it has no time for long-term planning; and that government today does not accept as its mandate development and control of its estimates and expenditures.
My remarks are not addressed to the problem of accountability of management to the responsible minister, important as that area may be. My brief remarks address the problem of parliamentary and government control of expenditures and programs.
My concern is that the present House rules, the legislative structure and processes, and government itself are inadequate, time consuming, inefficient, cumbersome and uncontrollable. People in our ridings perceive that an administrative monster has been created which devours almost $58 billion a year and is growing. The budgetary process, I suggest, has long since been free of any real input and control by Parliament.
I am also so bold as to suggest that a further step has been taken, and that is that meaningful input and control by cabinet over our expenditures has passed from the cabinet to deputy ministers and their senior staff. The proposition can be sustained that budget development and control has passed from cabinet to the senior civil servants.
All governments today have become large and their poblems numerous and complex. Their size and problems have increased but no real steps were taken to modernize and streamline government to enable it to deal efficiently with its new responsibilities. Governments have allowed themselves to become bogged down by administrative details, archaic rules and saddled with budgets they did not prepare in whole or in part and have no mechanism to control, except possibly after the fact.
Our 1980-81 estimates, which have been tabled, were tabled after the fiscal year began and will not be approved until the fiscal year end is close at hand and most of the funds already expended. I ask the members the question, who in fact prepared the budget and who is controlling it? I want hon.
Supply
members to ask themselves whether they really feel the estimates as tabled will be significantly different when they are finally approved by this Thirty-second Parliament in the fall. We all know the answer to that question.
As a new member, it is my position that our Parliament plays no meaningful part in the development and control of our annual estimates, even after the fact. It is also my position that the cabinet itself has lost, to an alarming degree, meaningful input in the development of our projected annual estimates and control of our expenditures. Only a revamping of our rules and modernization of the role of Parliament, its committees and the cabinet can give back to Parliament and the cabinet real control over the purse strings of this nation.
The Speech from the Throne says in this regard:
To increase the confidence of Canadians that their national institutions can respond effectively to their needs, my government would propose a program to make Parliament both more efficient and more responsive.
As a new member it is my position that Parliament plays no meaningful part in the development and control of our annual estimates, even after the fact. It remains to be seen whether the remarks 1 read from the Speech from the Throne are transformed into action by the Thirty-second Parliament.
What part has this loss of meaningful input into and control of expenditures played in the drastic increases in our annual expenditures and our national debt? Let me give hon. members just two examples of expenditures which in their conception were modest and acceptable but which are now out of hand and out of control. The items I have chosen were selected at random. One is large, the other small.
1 wish to discuss our foreign aid program and use the expenditure in this direction as an example of lack of control. In 1950 our foreign aid expenditure amounted to $10 million. By 1960 the amount had risen to $82 million and in 1967 it stood at $279 million. In 1980, Mr. Chairman, our foreign aid exceeded one billion dollars under the auspices of the Canadian International Development Agency or CIDA.
Some will say a large portion of our foreign aid is "tied" and that it brings back some benefits to Canadian industry and Canadian workers. That is correct, but we must remember that the industries concerned are the ones which are telling us every day that government is too big. We must also remember that the dollars coming back from "tied" aid go to industry, not to the government which granted them.
We must also bear in mind that our government is in a serious deficit position; it is borrowing money at high interest rates so as to make available foreign aid which this country cannot afford, using Canadian dollars which are borrowed and which drive up interest rates, thus causing inflation and driving up our deficit and national debt to serious proportions. 1 suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that this item of expenditure is out of control and has been for some time. This is an example of a good idea which has gone wrong.
1086

May 14, 1980
Supply
I do not suggest we should in any way duck our fair responsibility for foreign aid to developing nations. I ask only that the expenditure be controlled having regard to our deficit, our national debt, our unemployment and the general conditions of our economy in 1980. More than 15 per cent of the people in my riding are unemployed. We are borrowing to service our annual deficit and the national debt. We offer new programs or continue old ones on the basis of need, not on the basis of our ability to pay for the same. To explain: a family may "need" a new automobile but they put off the purchase until they can afford to pay for one. If national governments such as ours do not act in a similar manner, they will put in serious doubt the fiscal integrity of the whole country.
Hear, hear!

The same can be said about many of our provincial governments, for example, Ontario.
The second expenditure item 1 want to discuss as evidence of lack of control is the annual expenditure for the support of our peace-keeping forces in Cyprus. Mr. Chairman, in 1964 Canada agreed, quite rightly, to supply a portion of the peace-keeping forces in Cyprus. This was to be a temporary assignment-a matter of months involving a limited expenditure. But what happened? The six-month mandate for the force has been renewed by the United Nations Security Council 36 times between 1964 and 1979, and I am told by those close to the scene that there is no end in sight. The island remains just as politically explosive as it was in 1964 and all attempts to negotiate a settlement have failed. These peacekeeping forces have more or less become accepted as a permanent fixture by the Cypriots and, 1 am afraid, by many Canadians.
What has been the total cost to Canada of this item of expenditure since 1964 over and above the pay and allowances of the military personnel concerned? The answer is more than $36 million. In the fiscal year 1980-81 alone it will exceed $4 million and the annual cost is rising fast. I put the question: Who has been controlling this vast expenditure since 1964?
Pierre Trudeau!

It is an expenditure which in 1964 and perhaps for a few years thereafter was right and proper. Today it is out of control, as it has been for many years.
In December of 1978 when the Canadian ambassador to the United Nations spoke to the Security Council on the Cyprus question, he said:
We wonder how long the parties to this dispute can expect the international community to pour money and resources into a situation which they themselves do not seem to be working energetically toward alleviating ... our limit of patience is approaching.
Again I cite this small item of expenditure merely as an example, chosen at random, for discussion purposes today.
It is my position that we, as members of Parliament, and the government itself, have abdicated responsibility for the development and control of these massive expenditures amounting to almost $58 billion annually.
Hear, hear!

I say to all members of this House, in all seriousness, that this Parliament and this government must regain control over our annual expenditures. We must control our expenditures before the fact, not after the fact, and, needless to say, strict accountability is necessary and expected.
In my opinion, the next two decades will be years of no real growth in our GNP at best, and if there are reductions in the level of our GNP we ought not to be surprised. If growth is to level off or decrease, as I suspect it will, economies in government resulting from sufficiency in the supply of goods and services will not alone be the answer. There will be no landslide of new tax revenues-there is no need to look in that direction. We must gain control of expenditures both when they are in the process of being set and when they are being used. I have picked out only two expenditures at random to show that our expenditures are out of control.
Higher taxes are not the answer.
Hear, hear!

Better business management of departments of government would be helpful, but again that is not the answer, as I have said. We must get all expenditure items in line with our ability to pay for same. I have merely picked out two items in passing, so to speak.
How much time have we in which to take corrective action? In my opinion, the maximum time available to us is, at best, the normal life of this Thirty-second Parliament. The situation cries out urgently for remedial action. Time is fast running out. Moreover, in the timetable I have proposed no notice is taken of Russia's future oil shortage and that country's possible action to satisfy this shortage, or of any other scenario which would severely limit our oil imports. That is another story for another day.
Our national government collects and spends our taxpayers' hard-earned dollars. In our inability to control that process meaningfully our taxpayers, our business community and our Auditor General have little confidence. I for one-and I must say so regretfully-share that lack of confidence.
I am encouraged, as I have intimated, by the reference in the Speech from the Throne to steps which will be taken by this government, and 1 quote, "to make Parliament both more efficient and more responsive." I welcome such steps, as I know all hon. members will welcome them. As members of Parliament on both sides of the House we must work together to make our national government more efficient and more responsive.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make two comments, essentially. The first comment is one I have made before, and 1 am sure hon. members of the House will agree with it. That is that we are all concerned about efficient and effective management of government resources, both human
May 14, 1980

and financial, and I think the hon. gentleman who just delivered some interesting comments would be somewhat heartened if he had seen the progress which has been made, which is being made and the role played by the public accounts committee of this House in that regard under the very able chairmanship of the hon. member for Capilano, with you as vice-chairman, Mr. Chairman. I was there very briefly and 1 hope that progress will continue under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra.
As hon. members know, there is much being done, but it has not all yet come to fruition. The Auditor General has told us, and I think all hon. members will agree, that information is fundamental to re-establishing the control of Parliament over the public purse.
It was under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Capilano that a report was made by the Public Accounts Committee with respect to a new form of estimates. This proposal was designed to give information to parliamentarians, to the public and to the media in order to make dialogue in this House meaningful, because it will be informed dialogue. 1 believe we are making good progress in terms of the new form of estimates, and I hope that we will have some experimental forms for review and consideration, if not later in the current calendar year, at least in the current fiscal year.
1 remind the hon. member that we do have responsibilities to make certain kinds of expenditures and not to waste money. There are certain productive expenditures which we are committed to making. The hon. member has singled out the foreign aid program as an example of a wasteful expenditure. Hon. members will recall that it was under Prime Minister Pearson that targets were established to which Canada aspired to raise its commitment to foreign aid. I do not regard this as being a matter of an expenditure out of control. In fact, we have fallen substantially short of the target which was then set not just by Canada but by all countries which are concerned about the Third World and about problems associated with the plight of people in the Third World. Foreign aid is an essential part of our foreign policy, and I think it is important that we not downgrade its role by suggesting that foreign aid, which is now at something like .42 per cent of gross national product when we intended it to be much higher, is one of those kinds of expenditures which is out of control.
All 1 say is that the message of efficient government is well received. We are moving rapidly in that direction. But let us not attack expenditures at random. Let us not attack expenditures which are absolutely necessary to maintain some of the fundamental social programs which are so desperately needed by our citizens.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased that the minister does not think we ought to take programs at random. I want to ask the minister some questions.
I have here 12 CIDA projects. One is overrun $3.5 million in a $12 million project in connection with a railway in the Congo. There is another $4 million on a transmission line in Tanzania, and roads in Sudan. These are all overruns of
Supply
enormous amounts. The minister has copies of these. What is the minister doing right now to go back to departments to find out why there are overruns? What is he doing to insist that people who caused the overruns or who made misappropriations or "mis-estimates" on programs which were conducted are replaced in the public service because they are incompetent managers? What is the minister doing in this regard?
While the minister is looking at that, 1 remind him of section 5 of the Financial Administration Act, which deals with personnel management in the public service including the determination of terms and conditions of employment, which are his responsibility. Responsibility for all people who are employed in the public service is the minister's. People have given us cost overruns on a host of jobs. What has the minister done to get at that problem? When the minister finds out these overruns are likely, is he doing anything with respect to the personnel involved?

Mr. Chairman, first let me point out that CIDA has been the subject of an IMPAC survey, as I recall, and we hope, through the technique which I indicated earlier of signing off an action plan with the head of that agency, to bring about substantial or important changes in the management and efficiency of the funds which the agency disposes of. CIDA is in a particularly difficult position because many of the projects to which the hon. gentleman makes reference are shared cost or shared responsibility projects with foreign governments, and sometimes in those circumstances CIDA does not have the control which perhaps it should have in order to have a well managed program.
Remedial action has been taken with respect to particular projects which have been brought to our attention, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that as President of the Treasury Board my concern is every bit as great as his. I am glad to see that he has those concerns because when we bring forward proposals in this House to attack these inefficiencies and to improve these areas of management, I trust that we will have full support from all the other parties.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to hear that, and I am glad that the minister is in fact looking particularly into CIDA and cost overruns. However, he did not answer the question. The question really is, what has he done about it in terms of replacing people involved in the departments, in the ministries-in CIDA, if you like-who were responsible for approving projects which have cost overruns in some cases double the original amount estimated, in some cases triple the original amount estimated and in many cases 30 per cent and 40 per cent over the original amount estimated? Surely that is a matter not just of simple inflation or something of that nature. That is a matter which smells of malfeasance. What is the minister doing to replace those people?
Has he a program in mind to change that management type, as brought out by the hon. member for The Battlefords-Mead-

May 14, 1980
Supply
ow Lake who asked him about management? It was suggested that we have some of the finest working people in our public service, and the President of the Treasury Board suggested they were management people. What has he done about these management people who, in many cases, have worked on projects which have cost the government enormous overruns?

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member was a member of the public accounts committee, but I am not certain of that. In any event, I should like to point out that evidence has been put before the public accounts committee pointing to a lack of control in the past. This has happened on a number of these projects because of the inability to identify a person or several persons who are actually responsible for carrying forward a project. In the past, that has been a major problem. Under the major Crown projects policy, the project manager should be identified and accountability established. As I recall, the same is true under the policy on cost overruns which was published by Treasury Board when my predecessor, the hon. member for York-Peel, was there in August or September of 1979.
So the first step, before one can deal with personnel in terms of these cost overruns, is to be able to identify those persons who have been responsible. In the past that has been a problem. I hope that under the guidelines which we are establishing and the monitoring which we are carrying on that will cease to be a problem in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I was pleased when I heard of the appointment of the hon. member as President of the Treasury Board, particularly in view of some of his remarks in his book "Fiscalamity". I should like to quote from that book and ask if it is still his opinion. On page 15 of that book he wrote:
The act of 1917-
Referring to the Income Tax Act.
-was the head of the proverbial camel that finally occupied the whole tent. While it is true that there has been another war, the continuing need for increased taxes has not been brought about by war efforts alone, nor by a series of national emergencies, but rather by the attempt to fill the bottomless financial pit created by the welfare state since the Second World War.
Is that still the minister's opinion of the problem?
Of course, I was quite young when I wrote those words.
Oh, oh!
At least 1 had the courage to commit some of my thoughts to paper at that time. 1 think that that particular sentence taken out of context-
Oh, oh!

-is somewhat simplistic, but 1 do think that at one point in history, we moved too far too fast relative to our GNP. I think that the financial management of the affairs of this country in the early part of the decade left something to
be desired, and, quite frankly, that is one of the reasons I became involved in politics.
Hear, hear!

I must say that since 1975 I believe that the government has been on a responsible road, that gradualism was introduced to bring the growth of the public sector under control, to establish a trend with respect to government expenditures relative to the gross national product. So I like what I have seen in the past, and I hope that in my present role I will have some influence over continuing that trend in the future; in other words, in identifying social needs, ensuring that scarce funds are spent effectively in helping those Canadians who are most in need of help, and ensuring that in economic areas our priorities are on productive investments in the economic development so as to eventually increase our revenue base in this country and keep us on the road to prosperity.
Hear, hear!

I would say that most of us on this side hope that the President of the Treasury Board has some clout in the cabinet, but clearly some things have happened, such as the presentation made by the Minister of Finance last April 21, which indicate that the minister has no clout in terms of any reduction in expenditures.
We have a situation where the amount contemplated to be spent this year is over $60 billion, with a deficit of $14,165 million forecast. Clearly the only progress we have had since 1975 has been larger deficits, larger and larger public debts, and larger and larger amounts required to be borrowed.
If that is what the minister says is progress in the management of the affairs of the country, I wonder what he has been smoking. Surely if he still believes in what he said in his book "Fiscalamity", perhaps he should read his book again and get back on track. Perhaps at this point the officials in his department, or officials in the other ministeries, have captivated him, taken him over, or destroyed his sense of purpose in controlling accounts.
I should like to make some reference to the Auditor General's report, in particular to page 27 of the report, where the Auditor General indicates that on his test of a group which consists of up to 50,000 employees in the public service, the efficiency of their work was 60.8 per cent, as compared to the average performance in industry of 87.7 per cent.
While the minister is commenting on that, perhaps he would also comment on the transcript of an interview given by James Macdonell to Bruce Phillips, Ottawa bureau chief, on CJOH-TV on Sunday, May 4, at which Mr. Macdonell said he thought we have a fine public service, but that the system was totally upside down. Would the minister comment on Mr. Macdonell's remarks with regard to the wampum theory of government, if he remembers it, and would he say what he has done in the three months since he has been appointed President of the Treasury Board to attack the problem of reducing the number of people involved and achieving efficiency? Could
May 14, 1980

he also say what he has done with respect to the comment in the Auditor General's report that the public service, in terms of how it is operating at present, is operating only at 61 per cent efficiency?
1 must say I am flattered by the references to my book. 1 would not want to accuse hon. members opposite of infringement of copyright, but they seem to have photocopies rather than the original.
Oh, oh!
Those are briefing notes.

In any event, with respect to the point raised by the hon. gentleman regarding inefficiencies in the public service, the Auditor General did not say that the 61 per cent factor which he developed was applicable across the public service.
Second, the hon. member asked what I had done in that respect. Obviously I was concerned for a number of reasons, first, to determine the methodology, to determine whether one could extrapolate, as the hon. member has sought to do, to apply this across the public service at large. As I have said on innumerable occasions in the House, I am satisfied that one cannot make that extrapolation and that it is unfair to do so.
Going further as to what 1 have done, as he suggests, since the Auditor General tabled his report, 1 have held discussions at length with the Comptroller General to determine his appreciation of the Auditor General's findings. 1 convened a meeting with the Auditor General and the Comptroller General, with the opposition House leader, with the other hon. member whose constituency I do not remember, and with the hon. member from the NDP who has expressed interest and concern in this area. I believe we had a very informative and frank exchange of views on this subject.
What is your conclusion?

I am coming to my conclusion. The conclusion is one which I already expressed earlier this afternoon, and that is that there is much to be done in terms of the management of our public service, that the problem is a management problem. It is not one that exists because we have lazy clerical and regulatory personnel sitting around deliberately being inefficient. The problem is our problem as management and, hence, it is our problem as government and my problem as President of the Treasury Board. I inted to do something about it as soon as possible, hopefully through the implementation of the recommendations, to which I also made reference, in the D'Avignon and Lambert commission reports.

The minister in a press release, when he tabled his budgetary figures, indicated there was a total of 318,435 authorized person-years in last year's estimates, and that he was reducing that to 312,575. The minister, I am sure, is also aware of a table prepared by his department which
Supply
indicated the total number of public servants at the end of February as being 290,206.
Why has the minister budgeted or produced in his news release an indication that the public service needs to be increased from 290,000 to 312,000, an increase of 22,000, when in the entire year commencing April, 1979, continuing through to February, 1980, an 11-month period, at no time did the public service exceed 302,937 employees, even to the end of June, 1979? Why has the minister gone along with the departmental estimates of the number of people required when his own figures prepared by his compensation analysis branch indicated that in no way do we need that number of authorized people and have not had that number of authorized people for over a 12-month period?
While the minister is talking about that, will he continue to file and supply members of Parliament, as they were supplied by the president of the treasury board of the last government, with the quantum and numbers of people in the public service on the basis of their various categories of employment, so that we as members of Parliament can be brought up-to-date as to what in fact is happening and how many people are in fact being employed by the government?
It strikes me as rather strange that this minister would bring estimates to this House of Commons calling for the total employment of authorized persons of 312,000 people when at no time did he have anywhere close to that number working last year. Indeed, the maximum was 10,000 less than that at one point, and at the end of the year it was 22,000 less than he now requires. That is an enormous difference and I think the minister must explain that. He must explain his incompetence in this requirement. Why has he asked for this kind of money, particularly in view of the Auditor General's statement about inefficiency? There is something wrong here and we need an explanation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The President of the Treasury Board has a short period in which to reply.

It will be very short, Mr. Chairman, because I think the hon. member is comparing the proverbial apples to oranges. We are talking about two different things. We are talking about continuing, ongoing personnel on the one hand with the lower figure, and we are talking about person-years in respect of the other figure, which includes temporary help and so on. The authorized person-year figure is the figure I made reference to in the material which I tabled with the estimates several weeks ago, and that explains the discrepancy.
I will be happy to furnish the hon. member with an explanation. I think probably there is confusion in many minds because of that distinction, but the distinction seems to be obvious once it is explained.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to remind the President of the Treasury Board that as we all seek to control the expenditures in this country, and we must do so with determination and with zeal, we must keep a certain perspective as to how these dollars will be used. In trying to save

May 14, 1980
Supply
money we must be careful that we are saving it in the proper fashion and that we do not as a government retreat from some very important principles and ideas as to how to get real value for our money. That is another aspect of financial responsibility.
I suppose what I am really getting around to saying is that I wish to speak briefly on the decentralization process, where it applies properly in this country, because it has a specific significance to the Thunder Bay-Nipigon area, a very vast region, as we are so fond of saying, but an important one, as are all the regions of Canada.
Decentralization has a role to play not only for Thunder Bay but for the many regions of Canada which really want a potential for development. We talk about a strong Canada, and our Prime Minister has said we will have a strong Canada, but only as strong as are the many regions of Canada. I am trying to make a small point in relation to decentralization as it affects our part of the world. In the parochial sense we would benefit from some parts of the decentralization planning, but in the larger sense I think it is in the interest of the country to have these very strong regions.
We must take an area such as northern and northwestern Ontario as one of the many important regions of the country, recognizing that it is on the cusp, if you will, between east and west, and, therefore, decentralization is an investment potential for our area which would not only serve the people of Thunder Bay-Nipigon and northwestern Ontario, but also Canada as well in tying together the east and the west. We are the centre and we are a little of each; therefore we want to be strong in the centre. If we were a hockey team we would say that that is where a good team begins.
Therefore, I would ask the President of the Treasury Board to keep in mind in his deliberations, as we in Parliament must do, that while we must practise fiscal responsibility, we must think in terms of what decentralization can mean to the country.
It is foolish to overdo that principle, but there are certain offices-DREE would be an example-that function better when they are moved out into the country where we can have people in position, living in the area with an understanding of the area and the distances, for instance, of northwestern Ontario, those who have a feeling for the people, thereby being in a position to make far more rational and sensitive decisions for the area. That is one of the things I feel speaks well for the decentralization process. This is not a make-work process, because that is wrong and it defeats our attempts at fiscal responsibility. If we can legitimately put those governmental functions into areas where they have an opportunity to serve a real purpose by being closer to the people, then the people will in fact recognize this Parliament and this government as being more sensitive to the people, and that will help to increase the potential for development in areas of this country of ours.
So when we talk about expenditures, we must also think in terms of some expenditures which are not expenditures in the
true sense but are, in a business sense, investment dollars. They are the dollars that will help each area to grow and play a real role in Canada. As I say, decentralization has been a principle that has been expounded by this government, one I am proud to be a member of now and in the past.
I would like to reinforce the thinking in that area because we can truly bring the government closer to the people without creating more government. That too is not what we are after; we are looking for value for our dollar and the building of the regions of the country. From the point of view of northwest Ontario or Thunder Bay-Nipigon we feel there are a number a projects coming up which will rightfully have a role to play in the decentralization process. I hope that as we deliberate on the cost, on how we will use the moneys from the public purse and on how we will deploy our resources and the excellent manpower we have in our civil service to be of the most benefit, we remember that decentralization is an opportunity to expand the potential for growth and solidarity in this country.
I make it a very strong point to the President of the Treasury Board that, with all the trials and tribulations he will have and the questions from all sides that he will face as to why we are spending money here and there, he will recognize that there will come a time when he can legitimately say, "I can support this project because it is part of a necessary, logical and legitimate decentralization process that will serve the country well."

Mr. Chairman, I would like to reassure the hon. member that we share the views he has expressed, tempered, of course, by our concern with the cost effectiveness of every decentralization project. Each project must be examined on its own merits.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier as he pointed out the unfairness that some people engage, from time to time, in bureaucrat bashing. Unlike most Canadians I have had an opportunity to read the minister's book, "Fiscalamity." It has long since been remaindered at Coles, and it is very difficult to obtain a copy, but I would be very glad to pass my copy around and show it to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier. At the bottom of page 6 and at the top of page 7 the President of the Treasury Board dealt with the passage of what was Bill 259 by this Parliament. The sentence extends over those two pages and reads:
This was indeed the moment of triumph for the faceless technocrats and bureaucrats who lurk ambitiously behind Ottawa's political facade.
Does the minister feel that this is an apt description of the public servants for which he is responsible?

Mr. Chairman, the book was published in several editions. I am not sure to which edition the hon. member is referring, not that I deny the accuracy of what he has quoted. I am delighted that he derives pleasure from reading some of the things which I have authored. I have written a number of other papers, but not many books, if any.
May 14, 1980

The hon. member's quote must be placed in the context of the particular legislation with which I was dealing, the tax reform bill of 1971.

Mr. Chairman, Treasury Board would not be in the mess that it is in today if Don Johnston were still alive!
I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board a question with regard to the statement made in Toronto by the Prime Minister on January 12 while speaking to the Liberal campaign college. I have asked this question of the Prime Minister in the past and 1 have been unable to get a straight answer. The Prime Minister, while speaking on behalf of the Liberal party at that time, committed the Liberal party if it were successful in gaining the Government of Canada to holding down increases in spending to less than the increase in the gross national product. Will that commitment be kept, yes or no?

Mr. Chairman, I had interpreted the Prime Minister's remark as basically a repetition of the remark which was made, and which was written prior to that, I believe, back in 1976, when the view was expressed, and I believe it is still the view of this government and the Treasury Board, that the increase in expenditures would be kept within the trend line of the GNP. That is a significant undertaking, because it has been adhered to. One will find that expenditures from that period on have been substantially less than the cumulative GNP over the period.
Tell us about tax expenditures.

I am sure that the hon. member will have an opportunity to put his comments on the record in a more formal way. I think I have responded to the question, that it falls squarely within the context of the objectives set in the mid-seventies.

Mr. Chairman, after criticizing the spending plans of the Conservative government, the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister, committed this government which is in office today to an increase in spending which would be less than the increase in the growth of the GNP. Will that target be achieved this year? In other words, will federal government spending increases for this year, 1980-1981, be held to less than the increase in the GNP?

Mr. Chairman, on the basis of the evidence that I see, I would doubt that that could be the case. It could not have been the case under the fiscal framework of our predecessors in office either. But we do not know what the GNP for this year will be, and it is a bit premature for me to say whether it will or will not be more or less than the GNP. Certainly I intend that this government will try to attain the objective of staying within the trend line, and I think it will be within the trend line.

Mr. Chairman, we now know what Liberal promises are worth after they get into office. It is worth asking the minister about this point because Canadians are entitled to
Supply
a straight answer as to whether or not this government intends to keep the solemn commitment which it made to Canadians. My colleague from York-Peel has asked for five-year projections on federal spending. I will not even go that far. I will ask the President of the Treasury Board, who is responsible to Parliament for outlining the spending intentions of the government, what indeed will federal spending be for 1980-1981?

Mr. Chairman, as you know, we are dealing with the Main Estimates and Supplementary Estimates (A). The Minister of Finance indicated during his speech in this House some weeks ago that the projected total outlays could be in the neighbourhood of $60.4 billion. He also indicated at the same time that, depending upon the establishment of the blended oil price-which has been the subject of some discussion in this House-that figure could be decreased by as much as $1 billion, which would bring us down to $59.4 billion. That is the projection which was given by the Minister of Finance and I have no reason not to accept it at this time.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister then give a straightforward answer. The minister went out of his way when he tabled these estimates to say that they did not constitute the spending plan of this Liberal government. The Minister of Finance, when he smuggled in his mini-budget a few nights ago indicated that the projections which he was putting before Parliament did not indicate the spending plan of this government. Does that figure of $60.4 billion, with a possible decrease of $1 billion if the oil plans of the government are brought in, constitute the spending ceiling? In other words, wiP expenditures not be allowed to go beyond that ceiling?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is well aware of the new expenditure management system under which the government is operating. I can assure the hon. gentleman that the established envelopes will be within those ceilings and that that amount of $60.4 billion does provide for a reserve.
At an earlier time I took hon. members through the difference between the projection of $58.4 billion of the then minister of finance in December and the $60.4 billion. I think the hon. gentleman would have to agree that the events which have raised the amount to $60.4 billion have been in large measure beyond the control of this government and would have been beyond the control of the previous government with the exception of the $345 million assistance through the guaranteed income supplement payment. That is a new Liberal initiative which is included in that amount.

Let us make sure that the record is very clear so that we can look back at it in a few months time. Is the minister saying now that he will not come back to Parliament to ask for authorization to spend more than the $60.4 billion in this fiscal year?

May 14, 1980
Supply

Mr. Chairman, I may be an inexperienced politician but I am not sufficiently naive to ever say "never" on any subject. 1 hope I will be able to come back to Parliament and report that we have spent less than the amount in question.

Mr. Chairman, this minister is a one-man fiscalamity. Last Friday I put a question to him in the House relating to an unauthorized attempt to get into some 21 Canadian databanks operating from a location in New York City in the United States. Two of those databanks were located within the federal government. I asked the minister at that time whether he would table in the House a list of all federal government databanks which are hooked into the Infodat or Datapac systems.
Will he do that now and will he indicate what the contents of those data banks are? At that time the minister indicated there was nothing of a security or confidential nature in terms of the substance of the material contained in those databanks, so surely he should have no objection to tabling that material in the House today.

Mr. Chairman, following upon the request from the hon. member I have asked for that information to be compiled with a view to tabling it in the House. I might add that 1 am glad the hon. member asked the question because 1 intended to raise a point in the House and it is this. When I read my answer to the question posed by the hon. member, 1 saw that I had stated there was no sensitive material in any databank which had dial-in access. If 1 did not state that in those words, I certainly left that impression.
I should like to correct that impression, not by saying that there is sensitive material in those databanks, but to make it clear that the guidelines under which those databanks are operated do not permit sensitive material to be stored in them. I am not in a position, however, to give an assurance that there is no sensitive material in those databanks. That distinction should have been made at the time I answered the question. I am sorry it was not and I apologize to the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I know that members of the House will be very anxious to follow up on this question as to the nature of the material contained in the databanks for which there is a dial-in access.
May I ask the minister now about another matter. The Lambert and D'Avignon reports have both recommended stripping the Public Service Commission of its staffing functions and have argued that those staffing functions should be rolled into a reconstituted Treasury Board. In his 1979 annual report released a few weeks ago the Auditor General stated that he agreed with those recommendations. What is the position of the President of the Treasury Board?

Mr. Chairman, I touched upon the subject in some of my earlier comments. I have heard representations supporting both positions. I have not made up my mind with respect to that particular recommendation but it is obviously one of significance. It has been considered by the three sources
of which the hon. member makes mention, namely, the report of the Auditor General, the Lambert report and the D'Avignon report. We are seriously studying this matter along with the other recommendations contained in both those reports and I hope we will take a position with respect thereto at a very early date.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister about another aspect of his responsibilities. Two Parliaments ago, in her previous incarnation as minister of national health and welfare, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare responded to questions in the House about the use of the social insurance number as being "bizarre." She did not recognize the concern that many Canadians had about the abuse of social insurance numbers.
The government of which I had the honour to be a part put together legislation which it was intended to introduce to Parliament around Christmas or early in the new year which would have significantly rolled back the use of the social insurance number within the federal government. Does the President of the Treasury Board accept the decision made by the previous government to limit to six or seven the authorized uses of the social insurance number which may be demanded by the government from private citizens?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows, since he had responsibility in this area, there is a study by the privacy commissioner on the use of the social insurance number. I understand we are to receive a report with respect thereto by next August.

Is the President of the Treasury Board aware that the study by the privacy commissioner which was requested by my colleague Senator Flynn and myself dealt with the use of the social insurance number outside the federal government, namely, by the private sector and the provinces? What is the position of the President of the Treasury Board as the minister responsible for the use of the social insurance number within the federal government?

Mr. Chairman, it is my understanding that we have accepted the recommendations made by the hon. member himself with respect to the use of the social insurance number within the federal government. 1 understand that those recommendations were adopted by the previous cabinet, and as far as 1 am concerned at this stage those recommendations are being carried forward.
Mr. Chairman, when will we see the bill that was drawn up by the previous government to put into law the policy previously decided upon by the Treasury Board?
Mr. Chairman, I would have to consult with the government House leader, the President of the Privy Council, on that point.

Mr. Chairman, dealing with another aspect of the minister's responsibility, the Lambert report, the public accounts committee and the Auditor General have each
May 14, 1980

expressed concern about the whole question of accountability and direction of Crown corporations. The previous government of which I was a member introduced Bill C-27 which was designed to bring some control and accountability to federal Crown corporations.
What has the minister done about that bill? There has been no indication that it is being reintroduced since he took office and assumed his responsibility. What is the status of that bill? Does he accept the recommendations of the Auditor General in his 1979 report that action is urgently required in this area?

Mr. Chairman, I am currently reviewing the bill, plus recommendations and reactions to it and its proposed terms and conditions as they affect a large number of areas. A number of objections have been raised to certain parts of it, as the hon. member knows. It is my intention to bring forward a Crown corporations bill incorporating such amendments to the proposed legislation as may be necessary to resolve some of the difficulties which have been raised. I hope to do that at an earlier date. I also regard that, as the hon. member does, as a priority item.
Mr. Chairman, does the Crown corporations task force still exist and has the minister met in person with it?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, the Crown corporations task force does exist and I have met personally with Mr. Hy Calof.
Have you met with the task force?
I have not met with the task force but I have met with Mr. Calof and discussed the work of the task force. I look forward to receiving-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wish to confirm some discussions that we have had among the parties involving the hon. member for Yukon, the deputy House leader for the Conservatives and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Business of the House
Because supply business is coming out of government time today and tomorrow as opposed to opposition time, and as a rule private members' hour would normally be held tomorrow, we have agreed that we should suspend private members' hour tomorrow to continue through with the supply business in the spirit of the order that was made covering supply for the whole year, 1980.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is correct that all three parties have agreed to this proposal.
While I am on my feet, may I also ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council if we can be given the assurance that the other three ministers whose attendance we requested will be here tomorrow, namely the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be here tomorrow and as well I hope the Minister of Transport. He was prepared to answer questions this afternoon, but I am reasonably well assured that all three ministers will be here tomorrow afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I hope there is no inference drawn from the remarks of my colleague to my left and from the government representative that the President of the Treasury Board will not be here tomorrow, because we have many more questions for him. Hopefully we might get to one of the other ministers in due course, but we have almost a full day for the President of the Treasury Board for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is clearly the option of the parties. But perhaps members of the New Democratic Party would like to question another minister, and I think that was why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked the question. Hopefully those ministers will be available; I am pretty sure that they will be available. But whatever the Conservatives want to do is entirely up to them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The proposal has been made for the suspension of private members' business tomorrow. Is it agreed and so ordered?
Agreed.
